content: 1. Studies on video game use in children aged 4 to 8 and 13 to 18 years did not find an association with behavioral or attention problems, nor with parental-reported attention issues or antisocial personality traits. 2. Research on higher technology use (e.g., screen time) in children aged 4 to 8 years and 9 to 12 years did not demonstrate a link to behavioral or attention problems. 3. The quality of evidence for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was downgraded from high to low due to significant indirectness and the inability to assess inconsistency. 4. Evidence from cross-over trials was downgraded from low to very low due to the inability to assess consistency. 5. Longitudinal studies (14 in total) provided limited psychometric data on sedentary behavior items, except for two studies. A dose-response relationship was observed between higher screen time (TV, computer, video games) and unfavorable behavioral outcomes in 69 studies. 6. The quality of evidence from longitudinal studies was not upgraded from low to moderate due to a serious risk of bias but was upgraded for dose-response gradients. 7. Cross-sectional studies (12 in total) also lacked psychometric data for sedentary behavior items, except for four studies. The quality of evidence for these studies was downgraded to very low due to a serious risk of bias. 8. Sleep duration and quality in children and adolescents were examined in relation to sedentary behavior. A dose-response association was explored, but the evidence was limited and inconsistent. 9. A systematic review of 45 longitudinal studies found strong evidence linking child age to sleep duration. Moderate evidence suggested associations between screen time, past sleep behavior, and temperament with sleep duration. However, there was insufficient evidence for determinants of sleep quality. 10. Resistance training in youth showed potential benefits for metabolic function, but evidence was limited. More well-controlled studies are needed to determine whether these benefits are independent of changes in body composition. 11. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) was found to improve cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) in children and adolescents more effectively than moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). However, the optimal exercise duration and rest intervals remain unclear due to limited and inconsistent evidence. 12. Resistance training interventions may positively affect weight status in youth, but further high-quality research is required to confirm its role in obesity prevention and treatment. 13. HIIT interventions in children and adolescents were shown to be time-efficient for improving cardiovascular disease biomarkers. However, evidence for other health-related outcomes was less conclusive, and methodological limitations in existing studies hinder definitive recommendations.
